summary: For children aged 6–7, build the concept that 10 ones can be bundled into a single 'ten' and exchanged back again, with the quantity conserved across the swap. This unitising move — treating a group of ten as one countable thing while knowing it still contains ten — is the foundation of base-ten place value, comparison and column arithmetic. The central activity is a two-way physical/interactive exchange with proportional materials (a rod visibly made of ten cubes) and deliberate naming of the same pile as 'ten ones' or 'one ten'. Supporting activities anchor the equivalence with a reveal, probe reasoning through dialogue, and check retention.
misconceptions: Thinking a tens-rod is 'one' (counting bundles as single objects), so 3 rods = 3 rather than 30 — the core unitising error.
Believing the ten and the ten ones are different amounts (not conserving quantity across the exchange).
Being unable to reverse the bundling (can make a ten from ones but not break a ten back into ones).
Treating pre-grouped tens tokens as arbitrary symbols without knowing each holds ten.
Confusing 'ten' the count word with 'a ten' the unit.

activities.title: Base-ten exchange: bundle and break a ten
steps: Gather ten loose single cubes and join them into one tens-rod that is visibly ten cubes long.
Reverse the move: break (or separate) one tens-rod back into ten loose ones.
Watch or track a running count of the total cubes before and after each swap, and confirm it does not change.
Toggle/say the name for the very same pile two ways: 'ten ones' and 'one ten'.
Respond to challenges such as 'make one ten' and 'break a ten into ten ones, then give me 3 of them — how many loose ones are left?'
activities.insight: One ten and ten ones are the same quantity, named and organised two ways; bundling or unbundling changes the arrangement, not the amount, and the ten is itself a countable unit.

activities.title: Reveal the ten inside the rod
steps: Look at a tens-rod shown beside a pile of ten single cubes.
Tap or lift to reveal the rod splitting into ten cubes, with the label 'one ten = ten ones'.
State how many ones are inside one ten.
activities.insight: A tens-rod is not an arbitrary token: it holds exactly ten ones.

activities.title: Prove it to the doubter
steps: Respond to a character who claims 'three rods is just three' or 'the loose pile is more than the stick'.
Explain and, if possible, demonstrate why one ten equals ten ones.

Answer probes: 'If I snap the stick back into loose cubes, how many will there be — and how did you know before I did it?', 'Can you make a ten out of these loose ones?', 'If I only had nine loose cubes, could I bundle a ten? Why not?'
activities.insight: A ten can be counted as one unit that is also ten ones; the learner can justify the equivalence rather than only count.

activities.title: Check the ten-ones equivalence
steps: Match representations of a ten (ten ones ↔ one ten).
Answer 'a tens-rod is worth how many ones?'
activities.insight: Confirm the learner reliably recognises that one ten and ten ones are the same quantity.

checkQuestion: Put ten loose cubes on the table and, next to them, one stick made of ten cubes joined together. Ask: 'Is there the same number of cubes in the loose pile as in the stick — or is one more? How do you know?'
checkAnswer: They are the same. The stick is ten ones bundled into one 'ten', so 1 ten = 10 ones; joining them together doesn't change how many cubes there are.
